course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 2
unit.description: Follow the Spanish, French, Dutch, and British colonies, the regions of British North America, Atlantic trade, slavery, and colonial society from 1607 to 1754.

topic.title: Interactions Between American Indians and Europeans
topic.summary: How alliances, trade, and war shaped relations among American Indian nations and French, Dutch, British, and Spanish colonies, including Metacom's War and the Pueblo Revolt.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes relations between European colonies and American Indian nations in the 1600s?
choices: Constant conflict, because no European colony formed an alliance with any Native nation
Both cooperation and conflict, as colonies allied with and armed some Native nations while competing with others
Uniform cooperation, because Native nations accepted European rule in exchange for protection
Strict neutrality, because Native nations avoided involvement in the rivalries of European empires
questions.explanation: Alliances, trade, and accommodation existed beside competition for land and resources, and Europeans and Native nations used each other in their own rivalries.
choiceExplanations: French, Dutch, British, and Spanish colonies all formed alliances with Native groups.
Alliances, trade, and accommodation existed beside competition for land and resources, and Europeans and Native nations used each other in their own rivalries.
Native nations frequently resisted European control, and wars such as Metacom's War followed.
Native nations often sought European allies against their own rivals.
questions.distinguisher: Cooperation and conflict both occurred, so each wrong choice describes only half of the pattern or denies the alliances.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why many American Indian nations sought alliances with Europeans?
choices: They had been defeated in war and were required by treaty to ally with the nearest colony
They wanted to adopt European religion and government as soon as colonists arrived
They hoped to gain trade goods and support against rival Native nations
They sought to end trade with other Native nations and trade only with European merchants
questions.explanation: Native nations acted for their own interests, and an alliance could bring trade goods, weapons, and help against enemies.
choiceExplanations: Most alliances were chosen by Native nations to advance their own interests.
Native nations generally pursued alliances for trade, protection, and power rather than to adopt European institutions.
Native nations acted for their own interests, and an alliance could bring trade goods, weapons, and help against enemies.
Native nations continued trading with one another.
questions.distinguisher: Some Native nations were defeated, but the question concerns why many sought alliances, and the main reasons were trade and power.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a similarity between Metacom's War and the Pueblo Revolt?
choices: Both were Native resistance to colonial demands for land, labor, or religious change
Both ended with Native nations regaining permanent control of the lands they had held
Both were fought mainly with the help of French allies who supplied weapons to Native leaders
Both were fought mainly over control of the fur trade between Native nations and Dutch merchants
questions.explanation: Metacom's war responded to English pressure on land, law, and religion, and the Pueblo Revolt responded to Spanish demands for labor and religious change.
choiceExplanations: Metacom's war responded to English pressure on land, law, and religion, and the Pueblo Revolt responded to Spanish demands for labor and religious change.
Native power ended in southern New England after Metacom's War, and the Spanish returned to New Mexico.
French allies were not central to either conflict.
Neither conflict was mainly about the fur trade or the Dutch.
questions.distinguisher: The first wrong choice is partly true of the Pueblo case, but neither conflict gave Native nations permanent control.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains the outbreak of Metacom's War in 1675?
choices: Spanish raids from Florida had weakened New England's defenses against its Native neighbors
The Wampanoag had allied with the Dutch against the Massachusetts Bay Colony
The English had tried to take over the fur trade of the Iroquois Confederacy
English towns were growing and colonists were pressing on Native land, law, and religion
questions.explanation: Expanding English towns, English law, and pressure to adopt Christianity led Metacom and other Native leaders to resist.
choiceExplanations: Spanish raids from Florida were not a cause of the war in New England.
The war grew out of English pressure on Native peoples and did not begin with a Dutch alliance.
The war was fought in New England between English colonists and several Native nations.
Expanding English towns, English law, and pressure to adopt Christianity led Metacom and other Native leaders to resist.
questions.distinguisher: The Iroquois did trade with the English, but that trade was in a different region and not the cause of Metacom's War.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a long-term result of Metacom's War?
choices: Native nations regained control of the lands they had held before the war began
Native power in southern New England was broken, and many captives were enslaved or sold
England withdrew its colonists from New England after the destruction of several towns
The English and the Wampanoag formed the Covenant Chain to keep peace in the region
questions.explanation: The English victory ended Native power in southern New England, and many Native captives were enslaved or sold.
choiceExplanations: The war weakened Native nations in southern New England.
The English victory ended Native power in southern New England, and many Native captives were enslaved or sold.
The colonists rebuilt their towns, and English settlement continued.
The Covenant Chain was an alliance between the Iroquois and the English.
questions.distinguisher: The Covenant Chain is a real alliance from the same era, but it involved the Iroquois, not the Wampanoag.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

choices: ended Spanish rule in North America for good and opened the Southwest to the English
was a conflict between the Pueblo and French traders who had entered New Mexico
led Spain to abandon its missions and to stop all efforts to convert Native peoples
drove the Spanish out of New Mexico, and they did not return for over a decade
questions.explanation: Pueblo communities rose together, killed hundreds of colonists and priests, and expelled the Spanish until their return in 1692 and 1693.
choiceExplanations: The Spanish returned in 1692 and 1693, and Spain kept the region.
The revolt was against Spanish rule.
Spain continued missions after returning, though it tolerated some Pueblo practices.
Pueblo communities rose together, killed hundreds of colonists and priests, and expelled the Spanish until their return in 1692 and 1693.
questions.distinguisher: The near miss exaggerates the revolt's permanence, since the Spanish returned and kept New Mexico.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why Spain accommodated some Pueblo religious practices after 1692?
choices: Spanish priests no longer believed that conversion to Christianity was important
England had defeated Spain in the Southwest and required Spain to protect Native religious practices afterward
Pueblo resistance showed that Spain could not rule by suppressing Native culture and demanding forced labor
Pueblo leaders had agreed to join the Spanish Empire in return for protection from the French
questions.explanation: The revolt showed the cost of harsh rule, so Spain reduced forced labor demands and tolerated some Pueblo practices.
choiceExplanations: Spain continued to seek converts, though it changed its methods.
England did not defeat Spain in the Southwest at this time.
The revolt showed the cost of harsh rule, so Spain reduced forced labor demands and tolerated some Pueblo practices.
The Spanish accommodation followed the Pueblo Revolt, and it was not a bargain for French protection.
questions.distinguisher: Spain's goals remained religious, but its methods changed, so the first wrong choice misstates the change.

choices: an alliance between the Iroquois Confederacy and English colonists in the late 1600s
a treaty that divided newly discovered lands in the Americas between Spain and Portugal
a network of French forts along the St. Lawrence River and the Great Lakes for the fur trade
an agreement among New England colonies to defend themselves against the Wampanoag
questions.explanation: The Covenant Chain linked the Iroquois and the English in a diplomatic alliance.
choiceExplanations: The Covenant Chain linked the Iroquois and the English in a diplomatic alliance.
That describes the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494.
The Covenant Chain involved the English and the Iroquois, not the French.
The Covenant Chain was a diplomatic alliance with the Iroquois.
questions.distinguisher: The New England agreement is a plausible alliance from the same era, but the Covenant Chain involved the Iroquois.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the point of view of the author of the excerpt?
choices: A Wampanoag leader who defended his people's land against the spread of English settlement
A Puritan colonist who experienced the war as an attack on her family and her community
A colonial official who prepared a neutral report on the causes of the war
A French trader who watched the war while selling goods to both sides
questions.explanation: The author, Mary Rowlandson, was a colonist who lived in Lancaster, and she describes the attack from the viewpoint of a victim.
choiceExplanations: The author describes the attackers as enemies and is not a Wampanoag leader.
The author, Mary Rowlandson, was a colonist who lived in Lancaster, and she describes the attack from the viewpoint of a victim.
The author describes events that happened to her and does not write as a neutral official.
The author lived in Lancaster, Massachusetts, and was captured in the attack.
questions.distinguisher: The neutral-report choice is close because the passage records events, but its language shows a personal and hostile point of view.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 2.5, KC-2.1.III.E: British conflicts with American Indians over land, resources, and political boundaries led to military confrontations such as Metacom's War
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Mary Rowlandson, a Puritan colonist captured in the attack on Lancaster, Massachusetts, during Metacom's War, in her narrative first published in 1682
stimulusBlocks.citation: Mary Rowlandson, The Sovereignty and Goodness of God, or Narrative of the Captivity and Restoration of Mrs. Mary Rowlandson (1682). Project Gutenberg eBook #851.
stimulusBlocks.note: Rowlandson dated the attack by the older English calendar, which began the year in March. By the modern calendar it took place in February 1676.
stimulusBlocks.text:
On the tenth of February 1675, came the Indians with great numbers upon Lancaster: their first coming was about sunrising; hearing the noise of some guns, we looked out; several houses were burning, and the smoke ascending to heaven. There were five persons taken in one house; the father, and the mother and a sucking child, they knocked on the head; the other two they took and carried away alive. . . . Thus these murderous wretches went on, burning, and destroying before them.

At length they came and beset our own house, and quickly it was the dolefulest day that ever mine eyes saw.

questions.subskillText: Identify a source’s point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience.

questions.prompt: The events described in the excerpt were most directly a result of which of the following?
choices: A dispute between colonial assemblies and Parliament over taxes on colonial trade
Competition between French and English fur traders for control of the Great Lakes
Conflict between New England colonists and Native nations over land and authority
Efforts by Spain to extend its missions into New England from Florida
questions.explanation: The attack on Lancaster occurred during Metacom's War, which grew from English pressure on Native land, law, and religion.
choiceExplanations: That dispute belongs to a later period, and the attackers in the excerpt were Native nations.
The attack took place in Massachusetts and was tied to the war in New England.
The attack on Lancaster occurred during Metacom's War, which grew from English pressure on Native land, law, and religion.
Spain was not involved in the war in New England.
questions.distinguisher: The dispute with Parliament is a conflict between colonists and Britain, whereas the excerpt describes an attack by Native nations.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a limitation of the excerpt as evidence of how Native peoples understood the war?
choices: It was written long after the war by a historian who relied on secondhand accounts
It describes events that occurred outside New England and cannot show the war's effects
It was written by a person who did not witness the events that she describes
It was written by a colonist who describes the attackers from her own point of view
questions.explanation: Rowlandson recorded what she saw and felt as a colonist and captive, so the excerpt shows her view and not that of the Native attackers.
choiceExplanations: The author was an eyewitness whose narrative was published in 1682.
The excerpt describes an attack in Massachusetts.
The author describes an attack on her own town and her own house.
Rowlandson recorded what she saw and felt as a colonist and captive, so the excerpt shows her view and not that of the Native attackers.
questions.distinguisher: The eyewitness status is a strength of the source, so the wrong choices claim a weakness that the source does not have.
